title: Bookkeeping Basics for Small Businesses
summary: Learn to keep a cash book, record receipts and invoices, understand assets, liabilities and equity, and prepare a simple profit and loss statement and balance sheet.
audience: Small traders, students of business and anyone starting or helping to run a small business

lessons.title: Why records matter and how to keep a cash book

body.p: Bookkeeping means writing down the money that comes into a business and goes out of it, in an orderly way. Many small traders carry the numbers in their head. That works for a few weeks, then a supplier says you owe more than you thought, a customer says they already paid, and you cannot tell whether last month was a good month. Records answer these questions with facts instead of memory.

body.h: What good records help you do

list: Know your profit: money in from sales minus the costs of earning it.
Know how much cash you really have, separate from your own pocket money.
Prove what happened when there is a dispute with a customer, supplier or partner.
Plan: you can only decide how much stock to buy or whether to hire help if you know your numbers.
Apply for a loan or a grant. Lenders ask to see records, and tidy ones build trust.
Meet any legal duties to report income. Rules differ by country, so ask your local business or tax office what you must keep and for how long.

body.p: The simplest tool is the cash book. It is a table with one line for every time money moves. Money coming in is a receipt. Money going out is a payment. After each line you work out the new balance. This is called single-entry bookkeeping, because each transaction is written once.

Worked example. A woman who sells snacks starts the week with 500 in her cash box. On Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday she sells 450, 380 and 520. Total receipts are 450 + 380 + 520 = 1,350. She pays 600 for flour and sugar, 150 for transport and 200 for an electricity token. Total payments are 950. Closing balance = opening balance + receipts - payments = 500 + 1,350 - 950 = 900.

body.code:
Date   Details              Money in   Money out   Balance
Mon    Opening balance                              500
Mon    Sales                     450                  950
Tue    Sales                     380                 1330
Wed    Sales                     520                 1850
Wed    Flour and sugar                      600      1250
Thu    Transport                            150      1100
Fri    Electricity token                    200       900
Totals                    1350        950       900

body.p: At the end of the week she counts the real cash. It should be 900. If it is different, something was missed or a mistake was made, and she searches the lines until the difference is explained. A cash book is only useful if you can match it to the money you can touch.

body.tip: Keep business money and personal money apart, even if the business is only a cash box. If you take money for yourself, write it in the book as drawings (owner takes money out). Mixed money is the main reason small businesses cannot tell if they are making a profit.

body.p: Every line in the cash book should be backed by a piece of paper or a digital record. This is the evidence for the entry. The most common documents are the receipt, the invoice, and the supplier bill.

list: A receipt proves that money was received or paid. When a customer pays you, you give a receipt. When you pay a supplier, you ask for one.
An invoice is a request for payment. You send it when you sell on credit, meaning the customer will pay later. It shows what was sold, the price and the date payment is due.
A purchase invoice or supplier bill is the invoice that someone else sends to you.

body.p: Sales on credit do not put money in the cash book on the day of the sale, because no cash has moved yet. The money is recorded when the customer pays. Until then you note the amount in a list of money owed to you, which accountants call receivables or debtors.

Worked example. You supply 12 school bags at 35 each to a small shop. Before discount the total is 12 x 35 = 420. You give a 10% discount for a bulk order: 10% of 420 is 42, so the invoice total is 420 - 42 = 378. The shop pays 200 now and the rest in 30 days. The balance still owed is 378 - 200 = 178. Only the 200 goes into the cash book today, with a receipt. The 178 stays on your list of money owed to you until it arrives.

steps: Number every invoice and receipt in order (001, 002, 003). A missing number is a warning sign.
Write the date, the customer name, what was sold, quantity, price and total.
Make a copy: carbon paper, a photo on your phone, or a duplicate book.
Write the payment due date on credit invoices and check the list every week.
File the papers by month in an envelope or folder, and back up photos in a second place.

body.tip: Whether you must charge a sales tax or keep records for a number of years depends on your country and the size of your business. Do not guess. Ask your local business registration or tax office, and keep records for at least as long as they say.

body.p: To understand what a business is worth, we sort what it has and what it owes into three groups. Assets are things the business owns or is owed that have value: cash, stock, equipment, a vehicle, and money customers owe. Liabilities are what the business owes to others: a bank loan, a supplier bill not yet paid. Equity (also called capital or owner's interest) is what is left for the owner after the liabilities are taken away.

body.code:
Assets = Liabilities + Equity
Equity = Assets - Liabilities

body.p: The two sides must always be equal. This is the accounting equation. Every transaction changes the numbers but never breaks the balance. Follow one small business step by step.

list: Step 1. The owner puts 5,000 of savings into the business bank account. Assets (cash) = 5,000, liabilities = 0, equity = 5,000.
Step 2. The business borrows 2,000 from a lender. Cash rises, so assets = 7,000. Liabilities = 2,000. Equity stays 5,000. Check: 2,000 + 5,000 = 7,000.

Step 3. It buys stock worth 800 and promises to pay the supplier later. Stock is an asset, so assets rise to 7,800. The supplier is owed 800, so liabilities rise to 2,800. Check: 2,800 + 5,000 = 7,800.

Step 4. It sells part of that stock, which cost 400, for 700 cash. Stock falls by 400, cash rises by 700, so assets rise by 300 to 8,100. The 300 is profit, so equity rises to 5,300. Check: 2,800 + 5,300 = 8,100.
Step 5. It pays the supplier 600 in cash. Cash and the supplier debt both fall by 600. Assets = 7,500, liabilities = 2,200, equity = 5,300. Check: 2,200 + 5,300 = 7,500.

body.p: Notice the pattern. Profit increases equity. A loss decreases it. When the owner takes money out for personal use (drawings), equity falls as well. Borrowing makes the business bigger, but it does not make the owner richer, because the liability grows by the same amount as the asset.

body.tip: If your numbers do not balance, a mistake has been made somewhere. Check by recalculating each total, looking for a transaction written on one side only, and checking that you did not swap two digits.

lessons.title: Income, expenses and a simple profit and loss statement

body.p: A profit and loss statement shows how a business did over a period of time, such as a month or a year. It starts with income and subtracts costs. What is left is the profit. If the costs are bigger, the result is a loss.

list: Income (revenue or sales) is money earned from selling goods or services, whether or not the customer has paid yet.
Cost of goods sold is the cost of the stock you actually sold, not the stock you bought.
Expenses are the running costs: rent, wages, transport, airtime, electricity.
Buying a machine or a motorbike is not an expense in the same way. It is an asset that you keep using for years.

body.p: Cost of goods sold uses the stock that you started with, what you bought, and what is left at the end. Formula: opening stock + purchases - closing stock. In our example the shop starts with stock worth 1,500, buys 5,200 more, and counts 1,300 left at month end. So cost of goods sold = 1,500 + 5,200 - 1,300 = 5,400.

body.code:
Sales                                     9,600
Less cost of goods sold                   5,400
GROSS PROFIT                              4,200

Expenses
  Rent                                      900
  Transport                                 450
  Wages                                   1,200
  Airtime and data                          150
Total expenses                            2,700

NET PROFIT                                1,500

body.p: Margins make results easier to compare. Gross margin = gross profit / sales x 100 = 4,200 / 9,600 x 100 = 43.8%. Net margin = 1,500 / 9,600 x 100 = 15.6%. That means that out of every 100 of sales, about 15.6 is left as profit after all costs. Rounded figures are fine for planning.

body.tip: Profit is not the same as cash. If customers have not paid yet, or you spent cash on stock that is still on the shelf, your cash can be lower than your profit. This is why you need both the cash book and the profit and loss statement.

lessons.title: A simple balance sheet and an introduction to double-entry

body.p: A balance sheet is a snapshot on one date. It lists assets on one side and liabilities and equity on the other, using the accounting equation. Where the profit and loss statement is like a video of a month, the balance sheet is like a photo of the last day.

body.code:
BALANCE SHEET at end of month

Assets
  Cash                           2,400
  Stock                          1,300
  Equipment                      1,200
  Owed by customers                600
  TOTAL ASSETS                   5,500

Liabilities
  Loan                           1,500
  Owed to suppliers                700
  TOTAL LIABILITIES              2,200

Equity (assets - liabilities)    3,300

body.p: Total assets = 2,400 + 1,300 + 1,200 + 600 = 5,500. Total liabilities = 1,500 + 700 = 2,200. Equity = 5,500 - 2,200 = 3,300. You can check equity another way: the owner put in 2,500, the business earned 1,500 profit, and the owner took 700 as drawings. 2,500 + 1,500 - 700 = 3,300. The two answers agree, which tells us the books are likely correct.

So far each transaction has been written once. Larger businesses use double-entry: every transaction is recorded twice, as a debit in one account and a credit in another, and the two amounts are equal. Debit simply means left side and credit means right side. Debits increase assets and expenses. Credits increase liabilities, equity and income. Cash going out is a credit to the cash account.

list: 1. Owner puts in 3,000 cash. Debit Cash 3,000, credit Capital 3,000.
2. Buy goods for cash 800. Debit Stock 800, credit Cash 800.
3. Sell goods on credit for 500. Debit Customers owe us 500, credit Sales 500.
4. Pay rent 200 in cash. Debit Rent expense 200, credit Cash 200.

body.p: Cash is debited 3,000 and credited 800 + 200, so its balance is 3,000 - 800 - 200 = 2,000 debit. A trial balance lists every account balance. Debits: Cash 2,000 + Stock 800 + Customers 500 + Rent 200 = 3,500. Credits: Capital 3,000 + Sales 500 = 3,500. Both equal 3,500, so the books balance. If they did not, you would look for a mistake.

body.tip: You do not need double-entry to start. Use a cash book and the two statements. Accounting software uses double-entry behind the scenes, so understanding debit and credit will help when you meet it.

lessons.title: Petty cash and the bank reconciliation idea

body.p: Small everyday costs like bus fares, stamps and tea are paid from a small cash box called petty cash. Using a separate box stops you from opening the main cash for tiny amounts and losing track. The popular method is the imperial or float system. You start with a fixed amount, called the float. Each time someone spends from it they fill in a voucher with the date, reason and amount, and attach the receipt. At the end of the week you top the box up to the float.

list: Float: 500.
Vouchers: Bus fare 120, Stamps and envelopes 85, Cleaning soap 60, Tea and sugar 140.
Cash that should remain = 500 - 405 = 95.
Top-up needed to return to the float = 405. The 405 is then written in the main cash book as expenses.

body.p: The test is simple: cash in the box plus vouchers must always equal the float. If they do not, find the difference before topping up.

If your business uses a bank or mobile money account, your own record and the bank's record may show different balances on the same day. A bank reconciliation explains why. The usual reasons are timing: you wrote a cheque or made a transfer that has not cleared yet, or a deposit you made has not appeared yet. Others are items the bank knows about and you do not, like bank charges or interest.

Worked example. Your cash book balance is 2,350. The bank statement says 2,890. First update your book for things the bank knows: a bank charge of 20 is not yet in your book, so your adjusted cash book = 2,350 - 20 = 2,330. Next adjust the bank figure for timing: payments of 700 have not cleared and a deposit of 140 has not yet appeared. Adjusted bank balance = 2,890 - 700 + 140 = 2,330. Both are 2,330, so the difference is explained.

steps: Write the balance in your cash book and the balance on the statement.
Tick each line in your book against the statement.
List items in the bank but not in the book (charges, interest) and update the cash book.
List items in the book but not in the bank (uncleared payments, deposits on the way) and adjust the bank figure.
Compare the two adjusted balances. If they differ, check for mistakes or missing items.

body.tip: Do the reconciliation at least once a month. Unexplained differences are easiest to fix while the memory is fresh, and it is the quickest way to spot errors or fraud.

lessons.title: Stock records and a simple bookkeeping routine

body.p: If you sell goods, stock is often your biggest asset and the place where money disappears quietly. A stock record card or sheet for each main product shows what came in, what went out, and what should be on the shelf. Counting the shelf and comparing it with the record tells you about theft, waste and mistakes.

body.code:
Product: School exercise books
Date   In    Out   Balance
Start               40
Week 1  60          100
Week 1        75    25

body.p: Opening stock is 40 books. You buy 60 more, giving 40 + 60 = 100. You sell 75, so the record balance is 100 - 75 = 25. If each book cost you 18, stock at cost is 25 x 18 = 450. This is the figure used as closing stock in the profit and loss statement and on the balance sheet. Value stock at what it cost you, not at the selling price.

Now count the shelf. If you find 22 books but the record says 25, then 25 - 22 = 3 books are missing. Work out the cost of the loss: 3 x 18 = 54. Possible causes are unrecorded sales, stolen items, damage or giving out free samples without writing it down.

Pricing note. If you add 50% to the cost of 18, the selling price is 18 x 1.5 = 27, and profit per book is 27 - 18 = 9. Remember that a markup is based on cost, while a margin is based on selling price.

list: Every day: record each sale and payment, and count the cash.
Every week: update stock records, check the money owed by customers, top up petty cash.
Every month: reconcile with the bank, prepare a profit and loss statement and balance sheet, and compare to last month.
Every year: count all stock, review prices, and keep all documents safely for the period your local rules require.

body.tip: A phone spreadsheet or notebook is good enough. Choose a method you will actually use every day. Ten minutes of daily recording is better than a whole weekend of catching up each month.
